title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al., 2022)
content: ReAct prompts large language models to generate reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, so the model can plan, call external tools such as a search API, observe results and update its plan. Evaluated on HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld and WebShop. On the interactive decision-making benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, ReAct outperformed imitation and reinforcement learning baselines by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, using only one or two in-context examples. ReAct is the basis of most single-agent tool-calling loops.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (Shinn et al., 2023)
content: Reflexion reinforces language agents through linguistic feedback instead of weight updates: the agent verbally reflects on task feedback and stores the reflection in an episodic memory buffer to improve subsequent attempts. Reflexion reached 91% pass@1 on the HumanEval coding benchmark, compared with 80% for the GPT-4 baseline reported at the time. Self-critique loops of this kind are the conceptual basis for critic / evaluator-optimizer stages in agent workflows.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al., 2023)
content: The paper studies using strong LLMs as judges of open-ended answers. GPT-4 as a judge matched both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences with over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement as between humans. The authors identify key limitations: position bias (favouring the first or second answer), verbosity bias (favouring longer answers), self-enhancement bias (favouring answers generated by the judge's own model) and limited reasoning ability on maths questions. Mitigations include swapping answer positions and only counting consistent verdicts, few-shot judging, chain-of-thought judging and reference-guided judging.

title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment (Liu et al., 2023)
content: G-Eval uses large language models with chain-of-thought and a form-filling paradigm to assess the quality of generated text against defined criteria. With GPT-4 as the backbone it achieved a Spearman correlation of 0.514 with human judgements on summarization, outperforming previous automatic metrics. The paper also notes LLM evaluators may be biased towards LLM-generated text.

title: Building effective agents — Anthropic Engineering
content: Anthropic distinguishes workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents, where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage. Common patterns are prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer. In orchestrator-workers a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs and synthesizes their results; it suits complex tasks where the subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. The evaluator-optimizer pattern has one LLM generate a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop. The guidance is to start with the simplest solution and add agentic complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.

title: How we built our multi-agent research system — Anthropic Engineering
content: Anthropic's Research feature uses an orchestrator-worker architecture in which a lead agent plans the research and spawns parallel subagents that search simultaneously. A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research evaluation. Token usage by itself explained about 80% of the performance variance on the BrowseComp evaluation. The cost is significant: agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems about 15 times more tokens than chats, so multi-agent systems are economically viable for tasks whose value justifies the cost and that involve heavy parallelization and information exceeding a single context window. They are a poor fit for tasks needing tightly shared context or many dependencies between agents, such as most coding tasks.

title: Model Context Protocol — Introduction and architecture
content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, that standardizes how applications provide context and tools to LLMs. It follows a client-server architecture: a host application runs MCP clients that connect to MCP servers, and servers expose tools, resources and prompts. Messages use JSON-RPC 2.0. MCP defines two standard transports: stdio, where the client launches the server as a subprocess and communicates over standard input and output, and Streamable HTTP, where the server runs as an independent process handling multiple client connections over HTTP POST and GET with optional Server-Sent Events for streaming. Streamable HTTP replaced the earlier HTTP+SSE transport in the 2025-03-26 specification revision and supports stateless operation, which suits load-balanced, horizontally scaled deployments.

title: LangGraph overview — LangChain documentation
content: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework and runtime for building, managing and deploying long-running, stateful agents. Applications are modelled as graphs of nodes that read and update a shared typed state, with reducers controlling how concurrent updates merge. Key capabilities are durable execution through checkpointers, human-in-the-loop via interrupts that pause a run and resume it with a Command, streaming of state updates and custom events, and the Send API for dynamic map-reduce style fan-out to parallel nodes. LangGraph 1.0 was released in October 2025 as the first stable major version, with a commitment to no breaking changes until 2.0.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods (Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009)
content: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines the rankings of multiple retrieval systems by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document across result lists, with k = 60 used in the original experiments. RRF requires no score normalization or training and outperformed Condorcet fusion and individual learning-to-rank methods. It is widely used to fuse lexical (BM25) and dense vector rankings in hybrid search.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (Liu et al., 2023)
content: Language model performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context and degrades significantly when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts, even for models designed for long contexts. This motivates keeping prompts concise and passing condensed, relevant findings rather than full transcripts.

title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications 2025
content: The 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption. Indirect prompt injection occurs when an LLM processes external content such as web pages or documents that contain instructions. Excessive agency arises from excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy granted to an LLM-based system. Unbounded consumption covers uncontrolled resource use that leads to denial of service or runaway cost.

title: Claude on Amazon Bedrock — global versus regional endpoints
content: Newer Claude models on Amazon Bedrock are invoked through cross-region inference profiles rather than on-demand base model IDs. Starting with Claude Sonnet 4.5, Bedrock offers global endpoints, which route dynamically for maximum availability with no pricing premium, and regional endpoints (us., eu., jp., apac. prefixes), which guarantee data routing through a specific geography and carry a 10% pricing premium over global endpoints. Regional endpoints are required for data residency and compliance requirements. Availability of apac. profiles varies by model: for example Claude Opus 4.6 offers an apac. profile, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5 are listed without one.

title: Claude model pricing (per million tokens)
content: Base list prices per million tokens: Claude Opus 4.6 costs $5 input and $25 output; Claude Sonnet 4.6 costs $3 input and $15 output; Claude Haiku 4.5 costs $1 input and $5 output. Prompt caching and batch processing reduce effective cost. Cloud platform prices can differ by endpoint type; regional endpoints on cloud platforms carry a premium over global endpoints.
